spruce.e: From Middle English Spruce, an alteration of Pruce (“Prussia”), from Medieval Latin, from a Baltic language, probably Old Prussian; for more, see Prussia. Spruce, spruse (1412), and Sprws (1378) were terms for commodities brought to England by Hanseatic merchants (beer, wood, leather). The tree with this name was also believed to have been native to Prussia. The adjective and verb senses ("trim, neat" and "to make trim, neat") are attested from 1594, and originate with spruce leather (1466), which was used to make a popular style of jerkins in the 1400s that was considered smart-looking.

The use for unsolicited and unwanted email derives from a Monty Python's Flying Circus sketch. In the 1970 sketch, a group of Vikings in a restaurant repeatedly chant the word "spam". The earliest recorded real-life use for this sense occurs around 1993 which finds reference in a newsgroup post dated March 31, 1993, but the term may have been in use on "Multi-User Dungeons" (MUDs) in the 1980s.

spleenwort.e: From spleen + wort, from their use as a cure for anthrax in livestock. Cf. asplenium.

d.g: Great light, luster or brilliance.
d.x: What tho’ the moon—the white moon Shed all the splendour of her noon, Her smile is chilly—and her beam, In that time of dreariness, will seem (So like you gather in your breath) A portrait taken after death.

d.g: Magnificent appearance, display or grandeur.
d.x: The splendor of the Queen's coronation was without comparison.

d.g: Great fame or glory.

splendor.e: From Anglo-Norman splendur, splendour, or directly from its source Latin splendor, from the verb splendeō (“to shine”).

d.g: British, Canadian, Ireland, South Africa, Australian, and New Zealand standard spelling of splendor.
d.x: If the kind of network we envisage is to be established, it would be unwise to begin any of its services hurriedly with older stock, which, however admirable in its day, now has an air of faded Edwardian splendour that is out of joint with the times.

d.g: The surgical removal of the spleen.

b.g: denotes a surgical operation or removal of a body part; resection

d.g: inflammation of the spleen
Either of two flat oblique muscles which are attached to the vertebrae on each side of the neck and upper thoracic region and which draw back the head.

splenius.e: Borrowed from Latin splēnius, from splēnium (“a plaster, patch”) + -ius (adjectival suffix).

d.g: Enlargement of the spleen (process); an enlargement of the spleen (instance).
A junction or joining of ropes made by splicing them together.
The electrical and mechanical connection between two pieces of wire or cable.
That part of a bat where the handle joins the blade.
d.x: If the ball hits the splice, it is likely to dolly up for an easy catch.

d.g: Bonding or joining of overlapping materials.
To unite in marriage.
d.x: But come, it's getting dreadful late, you had better be turning flukes--it's a nice bed; Sal and me slept in that ere bed the night we were spliced.

splice.e: Circa 1525, borrowed from Middle Dutch splissen (Modern Dutch splitsen); akin to Middle Dutch splitten (“to split”), German spleißen (“to split, splice”), Spliss (“split ends, hair breakage”), French épisser (also from Dutch). The Dutch word originally referred only to the fraying of the ropes' ends but was then also used for the entire process of fraying and retying; hence the peculiar semantic development from “split” to “join”. The same development occurred in German.

d.g: A person or device that makes a splice.
A union of uniform spanning trees.

splicer.e: English splice English -er English splicer From splice + -er.

d.g: The act by which things are spliced.
The point at which two things are spliced.
present participle and gerund of splice
A cannabis cigarette.
d.x: smoke a spliff

d.g: To smoke a spliff.

spliff.e: From Jamaican Creole, possibly a blend of split, referring to the ready-made wrap, + whiff, referring to the smell of the smoke.

d.g: A long, thin piece of metal or wood.
A strip of wood or other material inserted into grooves in each of two pieces of wood to provide additional surface for gluing.
A flexible strip of metal or other material, that may be bent into a curve and used in a similar manner to a ruler to draw smooth curves between points.
Any of a number of smooth curves used to join points.
d.x: These conditions provide a framework which encompasses some notable approximation kernels including splines, so-called cardinal functions, and many radial basis functions such as the Gaussians and general multiquadrics.

spline.e: Mid-1700s East Anglian dialect. Origin uncertain but perhaps from Old Danish splind or North Frisian splinj and ultimately related to the root of splinter.

d.g: A narrow strip of wood split or peeled from a larger piece.
A splinter caught in the skin.
A dental device applied consequent to undergoing orthodontia.
A device to immobilize a body part.
d.x: [...] I saw in the white men's ward that little chap tossing on his back, with his arm in splints, and quite light-headed.

d.g: To split into thin, slender pieces; to splinter.

splint.e: From Middle English splint, splent, splente, from Middle Low German splinte, splente or Middle Dutch splint, splinte. Cognate with Old High German splinza (“bar, bolt, latch”). All ultimately from Proto-Germanic *splintǭ, *splintō (“piece of wood, splinter”), from Proto-Germanic *splint-, *splind- (“to split”), from a nasalized form of *splītaną (“to split”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pley- (“to split, splice”).

d.g: A long, sharp fragment of material, often wood.
A small such fragment that gets embedded in the flesh.
A group that formed by splitting off from a larger membership.
A double-jump bid which indicates shortage in the bid suit.

splinter.e: From Middle English splenter, splinter, from Middle Dutch splinter, equivalent to splint + -er.

d.g: present participle and gerund of splinter
The process or result of something being splintered.
plural of splinter
a handsaw for cutting with the grain of the wood
The situation of breakup or divorce.
d.x: A female couple I know were on the edge of splitsville until they discovered the wonders of Paperama.

d.g: Separated; no longer together as a romantic or sexual couple.

splitsville.e: From split + -s- + -ville, evoking a fictional town.

d.g: A person or a thing that splits.
A wedge used to cut logs down the middle.
A quarry worker who splits slate into sheets.
A scientist in one of various fields who prefers to split categories such as species or dialects up into smaller groups.

splitter.e: English split Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English splitter From split + -er.

d.g: greyish-brown moth whose larva is the potato tuberworm
An irregular-shaped splash, smear, or patch.
d.x: The consequence was that the stupid girl now had ended up with a bright blue ink splodge on her white “see through” blouse […]

d.g: To make a splodge; to render as a splodge.
d.x: Her features had been crudely handsome, too, like Millie's, but booze had splodged their outlines.

d.g: An irregular-shaped spot or stain.
To mark with splotches.

splotch.e: From a variation of splot (“a spot”) (compare blotch, from blot). More at splot.

d.g: To (cause to) gush; to flow or move in a rush.
d.x: The tomato sauce was splurged all over the chips.

d.g: To spend lavishly or extravagantly, especially money.
d.x: They decided to splurge on the biggest banana split for dessert.

d.g: To produce an extravagant or ostentatious display.
An extravagant or ostentatious display.
An extravagant indulgence; a spending spree.

splurge.e: Possibly from a blend of splash + surge, originally US. According to the OED, onomatopoeic.

d.g: A forceful emission of something, especially in small drops or particles; a spluttering or sputtering.
d.x: a splutter of water from a pipe

d.g: A forceful choking or spitting sound.
A noisy commotion.
d.x: But party carries every thing nowadays, and what a splutter have I heard about the wit of that saying, repeated with admiration about a hundred times in half an hour.

d.g: A disagreement or dispute.

splutter.e: The noun is imitative. The verb is derived from the noun.

d.g: United States pediatrician whose many books on child care influenced the upbringing of children around the world (1903-1998)
English potter who started a pottery famous for its bone china (1754-1827)
moths whose larvae are armyworms
The mineral lithium aluminium inosilicate (LiAl(SiO₃)₂), a pyroxene and ore of lithium, sometimes regarded as a gemstone, which may be greenish, yellowish or pinkish in appearance.
d.x: Two coexisting spodumenes occurred in sample A, one with high, the other with low, sodium content.

spodumene.e: From Ancient Greek σποδούμενος (spodoúmenos, “burnt to ashes”).

d.g: To ruin; to damage in such a way as to make undesirable or unusable.
d.x: All this sun spoils me for vacations in the far North.

d.g: To ruin the character of, by overindulgence; to coddle or pamper to excess.
To go bad; to become sour or rancid; to decay.
d.x: Make sure you put the milk back in the fridge; otherwise it will spoil.

d.g: To render (a ballot) invalid by deliberately defacing.
d.x: Dr Jonathan Grant (Letters, April 22) feels the best way to show his disaffection with political parties over Iraq is to spoil his ballot paper.

spoil.e: Latin spolium Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin spoliāre Old French espoillierbor. …

d.g: The part of something that has spoiled.
The process of spoiling.
d.x: To prevent spoilage, store in a cool, dry place.

spoilage.e: Latin spolium Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin spoliāre Old French espoillierbor. …

d.g: A spoiling or ruining; destruction.
One who spoils; a plunderer; a pillager; a robber; a despoiler.
One who corrupts, mars, or renders useless.
A document, review or comment that discloses the ending or some key surprise or twist in a story, or the internal rules controlling the behaviour of a video game, etc.
d.x: Good netiquette dictates that one warn of spoilers before discussing them, so that readers who wish to do so may experience the surprises for themselves.

d.g: A device to reduce lift and increase drag.
To mark (a document or message) with a spoiler warning, to prevent readers from accidentally learning details they would prefer not to know.
To tell (a person) details of how a story ends etc.
d.x: I've been spoilered, so I doubt I'll be able to enjoy the final episode.

spoiler.e: Latin spolium Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂yéti Proto-Italic *-āō Latin -ō Latin spoliāre Old French espoillierbor. Middle English spoilen English spoil Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. …

d.g: present participle and gerund of spoil
plunder; pillage
Someone who puts an end to others' fun, especially harmless fun.
d.x: I know I am a sad spoilsport, but it would make me wretched.

d.g: Like a spoilsport.
d.x: It may seem somewhat spoilsport to focus in on this negative after another important victory but to ignore it would be delusion. Southgate will not be letting it escape his attention.

spoilsport.e: From the verbal expression spoil sport (“ruin the amusement”).

d.g: a city in eastern Washington near the Idaho border
A Native American Plateau tribe who inhabited the eastern portion of Washington state and parts of northern Idaho.
The language of the Spokane tribe, a member of the Salish (or Salishan) language family.
A tributary of the Columbia River in Washington and Idaho.

spokane.e: A number of etymologies of the name have been proposed, most frequently “Sun children”, “children of the Sun”, or “muddy people”. According to Barry Pritzker (2011), these interpretations are most probably popular etymologies derived from an actual self-designation of Spokane Spoqe'ind (“round head”).

d.g: A support structure that connects the axle or the hub of a wheel to the rim.
d.x: The wheels were at first copies of a light hand-cart wheel, the wood spokes were brought together by tapering the spoke ends and wedging them together at the nave or hub and inserting the other ends in slots in the felloe or wood rim.

d.g: A projecting handle of a steering wheel.
A rung of a ladder.
A stick inserted into the wheel of a vehicle to keep the wheel from turning.

spoke.e: From Middle English spoke, from Old English spāca, from Proto-West Germanic *spaikā, from Proto-Germanic *spaikō. Compare Scots spaik (“spoke”), Dutch spaak and English spike.

d.g: A hand tool, mainly for woodworking, used to shape and smooth rods and shafts; often used in carving wheel spokes, chair legs, or arrows.
To shape or smooth with a spokeshave.
One who speaks as the voice of another person or a group of people.
d.x: One study of popular escapistic communications indicates that the recipients regarded the heroes and spokesmen as "trustworthy models and guides."

spokesman.e: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + man.

d.g: A person who acts as the voice of another person or a group of people.
d.x: Biden and his spokespeople have proudly touted his signature COVID relief bill as a major stimulus for policing in a national context already characterized by globally unparalleled police spending.

spokesperson.e: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + person.

d.g: A woman who speaks as the voice of a group of people.
d.x: Topps[…] has signed the Clique Girlz as commercial spokeswomen for Baby Bottle Pop, one of the Top 10 nonchocolate candy brands.

spokeswoman.e: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + woman.

d.g: The action of destroying or ruining; destruction, ruin.
d.x: There is much sad evidence, too, of the spoliation and dereliction of vanished industry: tips, slag-heaps and derelict colliery-screens among which the ubiquitous, nomad mountain sheep graze unconcernedly.

d.g: The action of an incumbent (“holder of an ecclesiastical benefice”) wrongfully depriving another of the emoluments of a benefice.
d.x: A Benefice is ſaid to be vacant de Facto, and not de Jure, vvhen the Poſſeſſion thereof is loſt by Spoliation or Intruſion, and the like: […]

d.g: A lawsuit brought or writ issued by an incumbent against another, claiming that the latter has wrongfully taken the emoluments of a benefice.
The intentional destruction of, or tampering with, a document so as to impair its evidentiary value.

spoliation.e: From Late Middle English spoliacioun (“looting, robbery, theft; an instance of this; (ecclesiastical) wrongful deprivation of the emoluments of a benefice due to another”), from Anglo-Norman spoliacioun, espolïacion, and directly from their etymon spoliātiō (“plundering, robbing”), from spoliāre (“to deprive or strip of clothing or covering, unclothe, uncover; (by extension) to pillage, plunder; etc.”), from spolium (“hide or skin stripped off an animal; (by extension) booty, spoil; etc.”). The English word was probably also influenced by French spoliation.

d.g: A word or metrical foot of two syllables, either both long or both stressed.

spondee.e: From Latin spondēus (“spondee”), from Ancient Greek σπονδεῖος (spondeîos, “associated with a libation”) from σπονδή (spondḗ, “libation”): spondees were often used in melodies sung at libations.

d.g: tropical trees having one-seeded fruit
Alternative form of spondyloarthritis.

spondylarthritis.e: From spondyl- + arthritis or spondyl- + arthr- + -itis.

d.g: Inflammation of the spine.

b.g: of or pertaining to the spine

d.g: A forward displacement of a vertebra over a lower vertebra, due to a congenital defect or injury.

spondylolisthesis.e: From Latin spondylolisthesis, equivalent to spondylo- (“spine”) + Ancient Greek ὀλισθάνω (olisthánō, “to slip, slide”) + -esis.

d.g: Any of various marine invertebrates of the phylum Porifera, that have a porous skeleton often of silica.
A piece of porous material used for washing (originally made from the invertebrates, now often made of plastic).
d.x: She removed Stranleigh’s coat with a dexterity that aroused his imagination. The elder woman returned with dressings and a sponge, which she placed on a chair.

d.g: The porous material that synthetic washing sponges are made of.
A heavy drinker.
A person who takes advantage of the generosity of others (abstractly imagined to absorb or soak up the money or efforts of others like a sponge).
A nuclear power plant worker routinely exposed to radiation.
To take advantage of the kindness of others.
d.x: The fly is an intruder, and a common smell-feast, that spunges upon other Peoples Trenchers.

sponge.e: From Middle English sponge, from Old English spunge, taken from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos).

d.g: hairy-bodied insect whose larvae feed on freshwater sponges
One who uses a sponge.
A parasitic hanger-on.
A person or vessel employed in gathering sponges from the sea.
A device for sponging cloth by means of a perforated adjustable cylinder.

sponger.e: English sponge Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English sponger From sponge + -er.

d.g: Any insect in the neuropteran family Sisyridae, whose aquatic larvae feed on freshwater organism such as sponges in the genus Spongilla and bryozoans.
The property of being spongy.
d.x: Actually the job was almost the despair of those early pioneers, for the surface was a "quaking morass," the surrounding district was undrained, and no sooner than soil was deposited than it was swallowed up, with no apparent effect, for the sponginess of the land remained unaltered.

sponginess.e: English spongy Proto-Germanic *-inōną Proto-Indo-European *-dyé- Proto-Germanic *-atjaną Proto-Indo-European *-tus Proto-Germanic *-þuz Proto-Germanic *-assuz Proto-Germanic *-inassuz Proto-West Germanic *-nassī Old English -nes Middle English -nesse English -ness English sponginess From spongy + -ness.

d.g: A neuroepithelial cell that develops into neuroglial and ependymal cells.
A blastoma composed of spongioblasts
A person or organization with some sort of responsibility for another person or organization, especially where the responsibility has a religious, legal, or financial aspect.
d.x: He was my sponsor when I applied to join the club.

d.g: A senior member of a twelve step or similar program chosen to guide an initiate and form a partnership with them.
d.x: My narcotics anonymous sponsor became my best friend when I finally was able to do something about my meth problem.

d.g: A person or organization that pays all or part of the cost of an event, publication, media program, etc., usually in exchange for advertising.
d.x: And now a word from our sponsor.

d.g: To be a sponsor for.

sponsor.e: Learned borrowing from Latin spōnsor (“a surety", in Late Latin "a sponsor in baptism”).

d.g: The state or practice of being a sponsor.
d.x: I find that for me, my sponsorship of a child via a charitable NGO provides a sense of great satisfaction.

d.g: The aid or support provided by a sponsor; backing or patronage.
d.x: The company provided sponsorship to the research team.

sponsorship.e: Latin sponsorder. English sponsor Proto-Germanic *skapjaną Proto-Germanic *-skapiz Proto-West Germanic *-skapi Old English -sċiepe Middle English -schipe English -ship English sponsorship From sponsor + -ship.

d.g: The quality of being spontaneous.
d.x: In any case, they are not very big on spontaneity. They sit on him for a few minutes before they decide what to do next.

d.g: Spontaneous behaviour.
d.x: Romney Leigh, who lives by diagrams, / And crosses out the spontaneities / Of all his individual, personal life / With formal universals.

d.g: The tendency to undergo change, characteristic of both animal and vegetable organisms, and not restrained or checked by the environment.
The tendency to activity of muscular tissue, including the voluntary muscles, when in a state of healthful vigour and refreshment.

spontaneity.e: From Latin spontaneus (“voluntary”). By surface analysis, spont(aneous) + -aneity. Compare French spontanéité.

d.g: The state or condition of being spontaneous; spontaneity.
An act of deception; a hoax; a joking prank.
A cyberattack involving deception via impersonated identities; a digital asset used in such an attack.
d.x: Don't click anything on that website! That whole site is a spoof! Call IT right now.

d.g: A light parody.
d.x: On Broadway, where it opened in 1949, Gentlemen Prefer Blondes was a spoof of the madcap Twenties which gave Carol Channing her first starring role; on the screen, it was an up-to-date spoof of sex which gave Marilyn Monroe her first starring role in a musical.

d.g: A drinking game in which players hold up to three (or another specified number of) coins hidden in a fist and attempt to guess the total number of coins held.
Semen.
d.x: ‘Holy-Jesus-fuckin’-Christ! I’m comin’! I’m shootin’ me bolt! I’m gonna fill ya twat with spoof!’

d.g: To ejaculate, to come.
d.x: [T]he release of semen from the penis predominantly symbolizes a forceful masculine operation, an orgasmic ‘rush’ – ejaculate refers to a sudden happening, an ejection – while the ‘loss’ of blood during menstruation is viewed as a more or less passive occurrence. Even the metaphors employed to depict these two aspects of corporeality serve to situate them on differently gendered poles. Man ‘spoofs off’ or ‘shoots his load’, while woman ‘gets her visitor’, ‘has got her monthly’.

spoof.e: Coined by the English comedian Arthur Roberts (1852–1933) in 1884 as the name of a card game involving deception and nonsense.

d.g: A ghost or phantom.
d.x: The building was haunted by a couple of spooks.

d.g: A hobgoblin.
A scare or fright.
d.x: The big spider gave me a spook.

d.g: An undercover agent, spy, or intelligence analyst.
d.x: The congressional study frets that Huawei’s and ZTE’s products could be used as Trojan horses by Chinese spooks.

d.g: A black person.
d.x: Some won't take spooks—hell, don't make no difference to me.

d.g: A psychiatrist.
d.x: Commonly, the surgeons view nonsurgeons with disdain. The most disdain is directed toward the “shrinks” or the “spooks,” as the psychiatrists are called.

d.g: A player who engages in hole carding by attempting to glimpse the dealer's hole card when the dealer checks under an ace or a 10 to see if a blackjack is present.
A metaphysical manifestation; an artificial distinction or construct.
d.x: He who is infatuated with Man leaves persons out of account so far as that infatuation extends, and floats in an ideal, sacred interest. Man, you see, is not a person, but an ideal, a spook.

spook.e: Borrowed from Dutch spook (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch spooc (“spook, ghost”). Cognate with Middle Low German spôk, spûk (“apparition, ghost”), Middle High German gespük (“a haunting”), German Spuk, Danish spøge (“to haunt”), Swedish spöke (“ghost”).

d.g: A reel; a device around which thread, wire or cable is wound, especially a cylinder or spindle.
d.x: If you need to reload film, the cassette can be rewound slightly by turning the hub located on one end of its spool.

d.g: One of the rotating assemblies of a gas turbine engine, composed of one or more turbine stages, a shaft, and one or more compressor or fan stages.
A temporary storage area for electronic mail, etc.
A splinter caught in the skin.

spool.e: From Middle English spole (possibly via Old Northern French spole, espole), from Middle Dutch spoele, from Old Dutch *spōla, *spuola, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ (“spool”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to cleave, split”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Spoule (“spool”), Dutch spoel (“spool”), German Spule (“spool”), Swedish spole (“spool”), Icelandic spóla (“spool; reel”). The aviation usage is based on the visual similarity of one of the spools of a turbine engine to a spool used for thread (especially in cross-section). See also spill.

d.g: An implement for eating or serving; a scooped utensil whose long handle is straight, in contrast to a ladle.
d.x: He must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.

d.g: An implement for stirring food while being prepared; a wooden spoon.
A measure that will fit into a spoon; a spoonful.
d.x: While Ms. Fly was with Sharon in the kitchen, Sharon asked the defendant for a “spoon of drugs.” Defendant refused and stated that he did not know where drugs could be obtained.

d.g: An oar.
d.x: To this class college rowing offers no attractions or place, nor are they generally looked upon by the artists of the "spoons" as a desirable addition […]

d.g: A spoon excavator.
A simpleton, a spoony.
d.x: To get all the advantages of being with men of this sort, you must know how to draw your inferences and not be a spoon who takes things literally.

d.g: A metaphoric unit of finite physical and mental energy available for daily activities, especially in the context of living with chronic illness or disability.
d.x: We therefore have to meticulously plan out each day with the small amount of spoons we have. Each task will cost us at least one spoon.

d.g: To lie nestled front-to-back, following the contours of the bodies, in a manner reminiscent of stacked spoons.

spoon.e: From Middle English spoon, spoune, spone, spon (“spoon, chip of wood”), from Old English spōn (“sliver, chip of wood, shaving”), from Proto-West Germanic *spānu, from Proto-Germanic *spēnuz (“chip, flake, shaving”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peH- (“chip, shaving, log, length of wood”). Cognate with Scots spun, spon (“spoon, shingle”), West Frisian spoen (“chip”), Dutch spaan (“chip, flinders”), German Span (“chip, flake, shaving”), Swedish spån (“chip, flake”), Norwegian Nynorsk spon (“chip, spoon”), Faroese spónur (“wood chip; spoon”), Ancient Greek σφήν (sphḗn, “wedge”)(though the connection to the Greek is likely impossible by modern reconstructions of PIE).

d.g: Any of various large, long-legged wading birds of the genus Platalea, in the ibis family Threskiornithidae, that have a large, flat, spatulate bill.
A species of fish, Polyodon spathula, native to the river basins of Mississippi, Ohio, and Missouri, or its extinct close relatives.

spoonbill.e: From spoon + bill, owing to the shape of the animal's beak.

d.g: spray blown up from the surface of the sea

spoondrift.e: Probably a variant of Scots spindrift. The Oxford English Dictionary suggests it is derived from spoon + drift (“mass of matter driven or forced onward together in a body, etc., especially by wind or water”), spoon being a variant of spoom (“to sail briskly with the wind astern, with or without sails hoisted”), but this is doubted by the Scottish National Dictionary: see spindrift.

b.g: mass of matter driven or forced onward together in a body, etc., especially by wind or water

d.g: A play on words on a phrase in which the initial (usually consonantal) sounds of two or more of the main words are transposed.

spoonerism.e: From Spooner + -ism, named after Oxford don Reverend W. A. Spooner (1844–1930), who is supposed to have habitually made such slip-ups.

d.g: present participle and gerund of spoonfeed
A plant, the yautia (Xanthosoma sagittifolium).
A plant, white arrow arum (Peltandra sagittifolia)
The amount that a spoon will hold, either level or heaped.

spoonful.e: From Middle English sponeful, sponefull, sponful, spone-ful, equivalent to spoon + -ful.

d.g: The track, trail, droppings, or scent of an animal.
d.x: Even poor Nobs appeared dejected as we quit the compound and set out upon the well-marked spoor of the abductor.

d.g: To track (an animal) by following its spoor.

spoor.e: Early 19th century, from Afrikaans spoor, from Dutch spoor (“track”). Akin to Old English and Old Norse spor (whence Danish spor), and German Spur, all from Proto-Germanic *spurą. Compare spurn.

d.g: A receptacle in ferns which bears the sporangia, usually a stalk, but sometimes a scale (as in horsetails).
d.x: The cones of Equisetum are sporangiophores.

d.g: A special type of hypha that bears sporangia on the tip.
A case, capsule, or container in which spores are produced by an organism.
d.x: Asexual reproduction by the production of a bud in place of a sporangium is not uncommon.

sporangium.e: From Late Latin sporangium, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”) + ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

DEFINITION 2. A field K is called a splitting field of a character χ of a group G if χ∈ operatorname Char_K(G), i.e., χ is afforded by a K-representation of G.
Let T be a representation of G affording the character χ. It follows from Definition 2 that K is a splitting field of χ if and only if T is equivalent to Δ, where Δ is a K-representation of G. In other words, K is a splitting field of a character χ if and only if a representation T affording χ is realized over K. Every character of G has a splitting field (for example, C is a splitting field of any character of G). If K is a splitting field of both characters χ₁,χ₂, then K is a splitting field of χ₁+χ₂, Therefore, in studying splitting fields, we may consider irreducible characters only.

d.x: I define spatial computing as human interaction with a machine in which the machine retains and manipulates referents to real objects and spaces. Ideally, these real objects and spaces have prior significance to the user. For instance, a system that allows users to create virtual forms and install them into the actual space surrounding them is spatial computing. A system that allows users to place objects from their environments into a machine for digitization is spatial computing. Spatial computing differs from related fields such as 3D modeling and digital design in that it requires the forms and spaces it deals with to pre-exist and have real-world valence. It is not enough that the screen be used to represent a virtual space—it must be meaningfully related to an actual place.[…] It is an essential component for making our machines fuller partners in our work and play.
